Matrices can be used to represent systems of equations, such as the following:

$$

For a $2\times 2$ system like the one above, we put the coefficients of the system into a $2\times 2$ matrix, called the **coefficient matrix**:

$$
A = \begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}{2}} & {\color{red}{3}} \\ {\color{red}{4}} & {\color{red}{-5}}\end{bmatrix}
$$

Each row has the coefficients of one of the equations in the system, and each column consists of the coefficients of one particular variable.
We also have the $2\times 1$ column vectors

$$
\mathbf{b}=\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{5}} \\ {\color{blue}{-1}}\end{bmatrix} \quad \text{and} \quad
\mathbf{x}=\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix},
$$

where $\mathbf{b}$ consists of each constant on the right side of the system and $\mathbf{x}$ contains the variables.
With these matrices, we can write our system as $A\mathbf{x} = \mathbf{b},$ or

$$
\begin{bmatrix}{\color{red}{2}} & {\color{red}{3}} \\ {\color{red}{4}} & {\color{red}{-5}}\end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix}
=\begin{bmatrix}{\color{blue}{5}} \\ {\color{blue}{-1}}\end{bmatrix}.
$$

We can write any system of two equations with two variables in this form.
Just to check that the above equation is true, let's multiply out the left-hand side to see if it equals the right-hand side:

$$
\begin{aligned}Ax & =\begin{bmatrix}2 & 3 \\ 4 & -5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}x \\ y\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}2x+3y \\ 4x\text{ }-\text{ }5y\end{bmatrix} \\  & =\begin{bmatrix}5 \\ -1\end{bmatrix} \\  & =b\,✓\end{aligned}
$$

We can calculate the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix $A$ using the following five-step algorithm.

**Step 1:** Find the determinant $\det(A)$ of the matrix.

**Step 2:** Form the **matrix $M$ of the minors** of $A,$ where each entry $a_{ij}$ of $A$ is replaced by its minor $M_{ij}\mathbin{:}$
   $$
M = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{M}_{11} & {M}_{12} & {M}_{13} \\ {M}_{21} & {M}_{22} & {M}_{23} \\ {M}_{31} & {M}_{32} & {M}_{33}\end{array} \right]}
$$

**Step 3:** Create the **matrix $C$ of cofactors** by changing the sign of some entries of the matrix of the minors according to the **rule of alternating signs**:
   

$$
\begin{bmatrix}+ & - & + \\ - & + & - \\ + & - & +\end{bmatrix}
$$

For each entry of $M$, we change the sign if the corresponding sign in the pattern is "$-$". Otherwise, if the corresponding sign in the pattern is "$+$", then we don't change the entry.

So, the matrix of cofactors is given by

$$
C = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{M}_{11} & - {M}_{12} & {M}_{13} \\ - {M}_{21} & {M}_{22} & - {M}_{23} \\ {M}_{31} & - {M}_{32} & {M}_{33}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

**Step 4:** Write down the transpose of the matrix of cofactors, $C^T.$

$$
C^T = {\left[ \begin{array}{ccc}{M}_{11} & - {M}_{21} & {M}_{31} \\ - {M}_{12} & {M}_{22} & - {M}_{32} \\ {M}_{13} & - {M}_{23} & {M}_{33}\end{array} \right]}.
$$

**Step 5:** Use the formula for the inverse of a $3\times 3$ matrix:
   

$$
A^{-1} = \dfrac{1}{\det ( A)}C^{T}
$$

In other words, we divide each entry of the transpose of the matrix of cofactors by the determinant of the original matrix (which we computed in step 1).

Let's see this in practice, in the next example.

We make the matrix $C$ of cofactors by changing the sign of alternate entries of the matrix $M$ of the minors. So, each entry $c_{ij}$ of $C$ equals

$$
c_{ij} = (-1)^{i+j} M_{ij},
$$

where $M_{ij}$ is the minor of the entry $a_{ij}$ in the matrix $A.$

With this and the formula for the inverse, we can write the formula for each entry $a'_{ij}$ of the inverse matrix $A^{-1}$ as follows:

$$
a'_{ij} = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)}c^t_{ij}
        = \dfrac{1}{\det(A)} c_{ji}
$$

Here, we used the fact that the entry $c^t_{ij}$ of $C^T$ is equal to the entry $c_{ji}$ of $C$ by the definition of the transpose.

The minor of the entry $a_{ij}$ in a $n\times n$ matrix is the determinant that we get when the rows and columns containing $a_{ij}$ are removed. For example, suppose that we wish to find the minor of $a_{32}$ in the following matrix:

One way to find the determinant of a $3\!\times\! 3$ matrix $A$ is to take the alternating sum of the entries of the top row of the matrix, multiplied by their respective minors, as follows:

$$
\det(A) = {\color{red}a_{11}}{\color{blue}M_{11}} - {\color{red}a_{12}}{\color{blue}M_{12}} + {\color{red}a_{13}}{\color{blue}M_{13}}
$$

Remember that we had to change the sign of the second product. When we multiply a minor of an entry by the respective sign in the formula like this, we get the cofactor of the entry. The cofactors in the above formula were ${\color{blue}M_{11}},$ $-{\color{blue}M_{12}},$ and ${\color{blue}M_{13}}.$

Using this idea, we can write the formula for the determinant of a $3\!\times\! 3$ matrix $A$ in terms of cofactors, as follows:

$$
\det(A) = {\color{red}a_{11}}{\color{blue}C_{11}} + {\color{red}a_{12}}{\color{blue}C_{12}} + {\color{red}a_{13}}{\color{blue}C_{13}}
$$

This is called the **cofactor expansion** of the determinant across the first row.

In fact, we can use a similar method of multiplying the entries of the top row of the matrix by their respective cofactors to find the determinant for any $n\!\times\! n$ matrix $A$ when $n \ge 3$. The formula is

$$
\begin{aligned}det(A) & ={\sum }_{j=1}^{n}{a}_{1j}{C}_{1j} \\  & ={a}_{11}{C}_{11}+{a}_{12}{C}_{12}+⋯+{a}_{1n}{C}_{1n}.\end{aligned}
$$

In general, for any $n\times n$ matrix $A,$ the **cofactor** $C_{ij}$ of the entry $\color{red}a_{ij}$ is

$$
{\color{blue}C_{ij}}=(-1)^{i+j}{\color{blue}M_{ij}}.
$$
